body.rationale: Governing IPS is still a draft, so I weight compliance as evidence but not as final. I am maximum_diversification (risk_structured) and excluded myself. The CIO needs portfolios that can be built on: those that meet the 8-12% volatility band and tracking-error budget, and whose weights lean on covariance structure over return forecasts, as the late-cycle finding in the paper suggests. First choice is resampled_efficient_frontier. It has no hard breaches, effective N of 13.3, Sharpe 0.41, TE 4.33%, and reasonable drawdown versus peers (-24.3%). It diversifies the estimation error that the reviewers hit mean-variance methods with. Its weak point is that resampling cannot fix biased CMAs, which is a premise risk and not a technical error. Second is pc_researcher. It has the highest ex-ante Sharpe among viable options (0.51), a backtest Sharpe of 0.70, a drawdown of -10.9%, and effective N of 7.2. Two reviewers flagged the volatility-band breach (3.82%) and the Sharpe above max_sharpe's 0.46 as inconsistent. That costs it rank, but it is a useful middle-risk anchor. Third is black_litterman, which is compliant with a 3.01% TE and effective N of 6.1. Reviewers found gamma-direction inconsistencies and a volatility sitting on the band floor. These are reporting and tuning issues, not fatal. Fourth is cvar_minimization, which is compliant, with the best backtest Sharpe (0.74) and a -18.7% drawdown. It brings tail-aware, non-traditional diversification to the ensemble. Concentration (effective N 2.9) is its cost. Fifth is max_sharpe, which is compliant with the best compliant ex-ante Sharpe (0.46). It ranks last because of the 46% us_value concentration and its extreme sensitivity to CMA noise, as its reviewers noted. Why first beats fifth: resampled_efficient_frontier delivers a similar return (7.11% vs 7.54%) and similar Sharpe at much lower concentration (N 13.3 vs 3.8) and lower drawdown. That makes it more robust to the CMA error that max_sharpe amplifies. I considered the cash-heavy risk-structured methods (hierarchical_risk_parity, risk_parity, inverse_variance) but all three breach return, volatility and tracking error, and my own proposal showed that cash degeneracy makes those weights unreliable. I left the adversarial_diversifier out of my top five. It is a single-asset vertex with three breaches, though it is valuable as an orthogonal probe, so I do not flag it. Bottom flag is market_cap_weight. Its -40.6% backtest drawdown and CRO risk of 0.80 are far beyond the limit, and its reviewers found the ETF-AUM proxy mislabelled as the market portfolio. The CIO should not lean on it.
